title: Shrinking a PDF Without Turning Its Pages Into Pictures
summary: Most browser-side "compress PDF" code does the same thing. It renders every page to a canvas, encodes that canvas as a JPEG, and builds a new PDF with one picture per page. It works on anything, and the file usually gets smaller. It also destroys the document: the text can no longer be selected or searched, vector drawings become blurry pixels, links are gone, and a screen reader finds nothing to read. For a scanned contract that is a fair trade. For a report that is heavy only because someone pasted ten phone photos into it, it is the wrong tool. The text and vector graphics weigh almost nothing; the photos are the only thing worth touching. This post walks through the second approach as we implemented it in the PDF compressor of VellumPDF, which runs entirely in the browser with pdf-lib and a canvas. Most of the work is not compressing. It is deciding which images you are allowed to compress. Images in a PDF are just streams An image in a PDF is an object, usually shared: a stream whose dictionary says /Subtype /Image , with its width, height, color space, bits per component and the filter that encodes its bytes. Pages do not contain the image; they reference it by object number. The same logo can appear on every page and exist once in the file. That gives you a clean plan: Walk every indirect object in the document. Keep the raw streams whose dictionary says /Subtype /Image . Decode the pixels, resize them if they are larger than needed, re-encode them as JPEG. Put the new bytes back under the same object number , so every page that pointed to the old image now points to the new one without being touched. With pdf-lib, step 1 is doc.context.enumerateIndirectObjects() , which returns [ref, object] pairs. Step 4 is less obvious. pdf-lib's JpegEmbedder has an embedIntoContext(context, ref) method, and if you pass it an existing ref , it writes the new image stream into that slot instead of allocating a new one: const embedder = await JpegEmbedder . for ( newJpegBytes ) await embedder . embedIntoContext ( doc . context , ref ) The embedder builds a fresh dictionary for the stream (width, height, color space read from the JPEG itself, /DCTDecode ). Anything the old dictionary carried is lost, which matters for transparency, as we will see. The eligibility list is the real work If you recompress every image you find, some documents will come out with wrong colors, broken transparency or invalid structure. Our eligibility function returns "leave it alone" for all of the following. Each rule exists because of a specific way to break a file. Stencil masks ( /ImageMask true ). These are 1-bit shapes painted with the current fill color, not pictures. Turning one into a JPEG makes no sense. An explicit /Decode array. It remaps sample values, sometimes inverting them. Re-encoding the decoded pixels and dropping the array would flip or shift the image. A /Mask entry. Either a color-key mask (an array: "treat these colors as transparent") or a stencil stream. JPEG is lossy and shifts colors slightly, so a color key that matched exact values stops matching. And since the new dictionary is built from scratch, the entry would be lost anyway. A soft mask carrying /Matte . A soft mask ( /SMask ) is a grayscale stream that gives an image its alpha channel. When it has a /Matte entry, the image was pre-blended with a background color, and the specification requires the mask and the image to have the same dimensions. Shrink the image and the file is no longer valid. So these are skipped too. Any filter other than DCTDecode or FlateDecode . JBIG2 and CCITT are bilevel formats that already compress black-and-white scans far better than JPEG ever will. JPX (JPEG 2000) and LZW are rare enough that we left them out rather than ship a decoder for them. Anything other than 8 bits per component , for Flate images. Flate images with a PNG or TIFF predictor. With /DecodeParms > , the inflated bytes are not pixels yet; each row starts with a filter byte and stores differences from the row above. You have to undo that before you have an image. We do not, so these images stay as they are. This is a real gap: images that came from PNG files often use predictors. Color spaces other than gray or RGB. We accept DeviceGray , DeviceRGB , and ICCBased with 1 or 3 components. Everything else is skipped: CMYK, Indexed, Separation, DeviceN, CalRGB. CMYK JPEGs deserve a special mention. Files written by Adobe software often store them inverted and flag it in an APP14 marker. Decode one in a browser, re-encode it, and you get an RGB image with colors that range from slightly off to photographic negative. Not worth the risk. One more rule sits outside the per-image check. Before the main loop, we collect every object that some other image references as its /SMask . Those streams look exactly like ordinary 8-bit grayscale images, and the main loop would happily recompress them. A soft mask turned into a lossy JPEG gets fuzzy edges and halos, so mask streams are never touched. Decoding, resizing, encoding Once an image passes, the pixels come from one of two paths. For a DCTDecode stream, the bytes are a JPEG file. The browser decodes it: createImageBitmap(new Blob([bytes], { type: 'image/jpeg' })) , draw it on a canvas, read back getImageData . For a FlateDecode stream, pdf-lib inflates it with decodePDFRawStream(stream).decode() , and we expand the gray or RGB samples to RGBA ourselves. If the inflated buffer is shorter than width × height × components , the stream is truncated or we misread it, and we bail out on that image. Then: optional grayscale conversion, a resize so that the longest side does not exceed a limit, and canvas.toBlob(callback, 'image/jpeg', quality) . Our default setting caps the longest side at 2000 pixels and uses quality 0.75. The step that matters most comes next: if ( newJpeg . length >= original . length ) continue // keep the original An image that is already a well-compressed JPEG, or a small flat-color Flate image, can come out larger after re-encoding. We only swap when the result is lighter. Without this check, "compression" makes some files grow. If the original image had a soft mask, we put the reference back on the new dictionary after embedding: const smask = dict . get ( PDFName . of ( ' SMask ' )) await embedder . embedIntoContext ( context , ref ) if ( smask ) context . lookup ( ref , PDFStream ). dict . set ( PDFName . of ( ' SMask ' ), smask ) A decode or encode failure on a single image (a damaged progressive JPEG, for instance) is caught and skipped. One bad image should not fail the whole document. Finally the document is saved with doc.save({ useObjectStreams: true }) , which packs the small non-stream objects into compressed object streams. On its own, that re-save is our lossless "Light" level, which can save a little on files written by tools that did not use object streams. The grayscale trap Our "grayscale images" option has a limit worth knowing. The canvas JPEG encoder only writes three-component JPEGs. Set R = G = B on every pixel and the image looks gray, but the file keeps three channels, and pdf-lib tags it DeviceRGB . You lose the color without saving the bytes a one-channel JPEG would save. Real single-channel output means shipping your own JPEG encoder. Hitting a target size without compounding damage People rarely want "compress at level 2". They want "under 2 MB, because the upload form says so". Our target-size mode tries settings in order: first image recompression with progressively stricter limits (2000 px at 0.75, then 1600 px at 0.6, 1200 px at 0.45, 900 px at 0.3), and only after that, as a last resort, full-page rasterization at decreasing scales. Two details made this behave well. Every attempt starts from the original bytes. It is tempting to feed attempt N's output into attempt N+1. That re-encodes JPEGs that were already re-encoded, and each pass adds artifacts on top of the previous ones. Reloading the original is slower and gives a cleaner result at the same size. The best result is kept even if the target is missed, and the user is told. The interface says plainly whether the target was reached, and shows a separate warning when reaching it required converting pages to images, because at that point the text is no longer selectable. If the output is heavier than the input, a "Keep the original" button appears. Silently delivering a worse file is the failure mode to avoid. Keeping the PDF logic testable The module that walks the PDF never imports a canvas. The JPEG decoder and encoder are passed in as functions. In the browser they wrap createImageBitmap and canvas.toBlob . In a Node test they wrap @napi-rs/canvas . Everything else (object traversal, eligibility, stream replacement, the size comparison) is plain JavaScript that runs under Node against real PDF files, without a browser. That split matters because the eligibility rules are where the bugs hide, and the cases worth checking (a CMYK JPEG, a masked image, a predictor-encoded Flate stream) are much easier to feed to a Node script than to click through in a browser. Try it on a real file If you want to see the behavior on your own files, the compressor runs locally in the tab, next to the other free PDF tools on VellumPDF . Try a document with selectable text on the default level, then on "Maximum", and compare what you can still copy out of each.

title: Saved to Postgres, never queued: the transactional outbox for Node
summary: Here's a bug that never shows up in tests. A request saves an order to Postgres, then calls queue.add('send-receipt', ...) . The deploy restarts the pod between those two lines, or Redis blips for two seconds, and now you have a paid order that never gets a receipt, an invoice or a warehouse pick. Nothing errors. Nothing retries. The two writes were never one unit, and nobody notices until a customer emails. I'm Krrish Kumar, a backend engineer. I wrote this with AI assistance for drafting and editing; the code and every number below come from a test script I ran against PostgreSQL 18.6 and Redis, with BullMQ 5.81.5 and 6.5.3. The fix is an old pattern called the transactional outbox, and this post builds a small version of it in Node, plus the three mistakes I made on the way. Why "just retry" doesn't work There are two orders you can write in, and both are broken: You do Crash between the two writes Result COMMIT , then queue.add() after the commit Order saved, job never created queue.add() , then COMMIT after the add Job runs for an order that was rolled back You can't wrap Redis and Postgres in one transaction. Even BullMQ 6, which can now keep its queues in PostgreSQL, doesn't help here: its backend interface "intentionally exposes no connection or transaction type", so queue.add() runs on its own connection, outside your transaction. The outbox gets around this by not writing to the queue in the request at all. The request writes the order and a row describing the job in the same database transaction. A separate relay process copies outbox rows into the queue later. If the transaction commits, both rows exist. If it rolls back, neither does. The table CREATE TABLE outbox ( id bigserial PRIMARY KEY , topic text NOT NULL , payload jsonb NOT NULL , created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now (), published_at timestamptz ); -- Only unpublished rows are indexed, so the relay's query stays cheap -- even when the table holds millions of published rows. CREATE INDEX outbox_unpublished ON outbox ( id ) WHERE published_at IS NULL ; The write side export async function createOrder ( pool , { customer , totalPaise }) { const client = await pool . connect (); try { await client . query ( ' BEGIN ' ); const { rows : [ order ] } = await client . query ( ' INSERT INTO orders (customer, total_paise) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING id ' , [ customer , totalPaise ], ); await client . query ( `INSERT INTO outbox (topic, payload) VALUES ('order.created', $1)` , [{ orderId : order . id , customer }], ); await client . query ( ' NOTIFY outbox ' ); // delivered only if the transaction commits await client . query ( ' COMMIT ' ); return order . id ; } catch ( err ) { await client . query ( ' ROLLBACK ' ); throw err ; } finally { client . release (); } } The NOTIFY is optional, and it's free: Postgres holds notifications sent inside a transaction until it commits, and drops them on rollback. The relay uses it to wake up immediately instead of waiting for its next poll. The relay export async function relayBatch ( pool , queue , { limit = 100 } = {}) { const client = await pool . connect (); try { await client . query ( ' BEGIN ' ); const { rows } = await client . query ( `SELECT id, topic, payload FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT $1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` , [ limit ], ); for ( const row of rows ) { await queue . add ( row . topic , row . payload , { jobId : `outbox- ${ row . id } ` }); } await client . query ( ' UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE id = ANY($1) ' , [ rows . map (( r ) => r . id )], ); await client . query ( ' COMMIT ' ); return rows . length ; } catch ( err ) { await client . query ( ' ROLLBACK ' ). catch (() => {}); throw err ; } finally { client . release (); } } Three things carry the weight here: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets you run more than one relay. Each one locks the rows it picked, and the others skip them instead of waiting. In my test, 4 relays drained 500 rows with exactly 500 queue.add() calls between them, split 100/150/150/100. The row is marked published only after the add succeeds. If the process dies after queue.add() but before COMMIT , the transaction rolls back, the lock goes away, and the next run picks the same row again. That means the relay is at least once : the same row can reach the queue twice. jobId: outbox- is what makes "twice" harmless. BullMQ ignores an add() whose jobId already exists. I simulated the crash (throw after the adds, before the commit), ran the relay again, and the queue held one job, not two. One trade-off: the transaction stays open while you talk to Redis. With a batch of 100 that's a few milliseconds, but keep batches small so one slow Redis call doesn't hold locks for long. The loop around it drains, then sleeps until a NOTIFY arrives or a poll timer fires, whichever comes first: export async function runRelay ( pool , queue , { pollMs = 5000 , signal } = {}) { const listener = await pool . connect (); let wake ; const nudge = () => wake ?.(); listener . on ( ' notification ' , nudge ); await listener . query ( ' LISTEN outbox ' ); try { while ( ! signal ?. aborted ) { while (( await relayBatch ( pool , queue )) > 0 ) {} await new Promise (( resolve ) => { wake = resolve ; setTimeout ( resolve , pollMs ); signal ?. addEventListener ( ' abort ' , resolve , { once : true }); }); } } finally { listener . removeListener ( ' notification ' , nudge ); await listener . query ( ' UNLISTEN outbox ' ). catch (() => {}); listener . release (); } } With the poll timer set to 60 seconds, a new order was in the queue 9 ms after its commit, so NOTIFY did the work. Keep the poll anyway. A notification sent while the relay is reconnecting is simply lost, and the poll is what catches it. Mistake 1: a "last seen id" cursor My first relay remembered the highest id it had published and asked for WHERE id > $lastSeen . It looks fine, and it loses rows. bigserial hands out ids when a row is inserted , not when its transaction commits . Transaction A inserts id 1 and is still working. Transaction B inserts id 2 and commits. The relay reads, sees only id 2, and sets lastSeen = 2 . Then A commits. Id 1 is now in the table, and id > 2 will never return it. My test reproduced it: the first read saw [2] , the second saw [] , and row 1 was stuck forever. Asking WHERE published_at IS NULL instead has no cursor to get ahead of. The same test with that query published both rows. Mistake 2: removeOnComplete: true The jobId dedupe only works while BullMQ still has the job. With removeOnComplete: true (or { count: 0 } ), a completed job is deleted at once, and a later add() with the same jobId is treated as new. In my test the processor ran twice for outbox-1 . That matters for the outbox, because the duplicate add comes from a relay retry, and the first job may already be done by then. Keep completed jobs for longer than any retry could take: const worker = new Worker ( ' orders ' , processor , { connection , removeOnComplete : { age : 24 * 3600 }, // seconds }); With that setting, a second add() of the same jobId inside the window was ignored, and the processor ran once. This narrows the window but doesn't close it. If your consumer sends money or email, have it check orderId before acting too. Mistake 3: a colon in the jobId I reached for a colon out of habit. BullMQ rejects it: Custom Id cannot contain : , because : is its Redis key separator. A bare number fails too, with Custom Id cannot be integers , so jobId: String(row.id) doesn't work either. A prefix with a dash ( outbox-42 ) passes both checks, on BullMQ 5 and 6. I hit mistakes 2 and 3 often enough that I wrote lint rules for them in eslint-plugin-bullmq, a small plugin I maintain. On a file that sets jobId: `outbox:${row.id}` together with removeOnComplete: true , it reports both: 5:52 error BullMQ uses ':' as its Redis key separator, so a custom jobId containing ':' is rejected ... bullmq/valid-job-id 5:72 warning removeOnComplete: true deletes the job as soon as it finishes, so a later add() with the same jobId runs again ... bullmq/no-jobid-dedupe-with-remove-on-complete You don't need it for any of this. A code review checklist with the same two lines works too. Cleaning up Published rows pile up. Delete them in batches from a daily job, so one big DELETE doesn't hold locks or bloat the table: DELETE FROM outbox WHERE id IN ( SELECT id FROM outbox WHERE published_at now () - interval '7 days' LIMIT 5000 ); Run it in a loop until it deletes 0 rows. Keep the retention longer than your BullMQ removeOnComplete age, so you can still trace a job back to its row. When you don't need this If losing an occasional job is fine (analytics pings, cache warming), skip the outbox. If the work can live entirely in Postgres, a Postgres-backed job queue that shares your connection, such as graphile-worker or pg-boss, can enqueue inside your own transaction, and you get the same guarantee without a relay. The outbox is for when the job has to land somewhere else: Redis, Kafka, a webhook, another service. Checklist Write the business row and the outbox row in one transaction. Never call the queue from the request. Relay with WHERE published_at IS NULL ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED , not an id cursor. Mark rows published only after the queue accepted them, and expect duplicates. Use a deterministic jobId with no : and not a bare number. Keep completed jobs longer than a relay retry could take, and make consumers idempotent anyway. NOTIFY for speed, poll for safety. Delete published rows in batches. Disclosure: I'm Krrish Kumar, and I maintain eslint-plugin-bullmq . The test script behind the numbers here ran on PostgreSQL 18.6, BullMQ 5.81.5 and 6.5.3, ioredis and node-postgres.

title: No cloud to lean on: building a reliable data platform on a bank's own servers
summary: Replication, failover, graceful shutdown, autoscaling and alerting usually arrive as managed services. Inside a bank, you build them from Kubernetes, an operator or two and a lot of small decisions. Here is how each one works, with the code. Field notes from moving a transaction reconciliation platform from AWS onto Kubernetes inside banks' data centres The constraints Five words, one goal Reliability: no work is lost silently Fault tolerance: replication, redundancy, failover, graceful degradation High availability: what survives what Scalability on a fixed number of servers Monitoring and observability without the internet High availability is not a backup Checklist The constraints In the cloud, our reconciliation platform ran on managed pieces: a managed database with automatic failover, managed queues, managed object storage, autoscaling groups and a monitoring SaaS. Banks wanted the same platform on their own hardware and their hardware comes with rules: No internet. Images come from the bank's registry, backups go to the bank's storage and the only way out is the bank's mail relay. A fixed number of servers. Three to seven machines, sized months in advance. Nothing appears when load goes up. No managed services. Every database, queue and object store runs inside the cluster, so failover is our problem. Little access. The people on call may not have cluster access and our engineers get in only through a bastion, when the bank allows it. The platform itself is a typical event-driven data system. Users upload files through a web portal. Workers clean them, an ingestion engine loads them into an Iceberg data lake with Spark and reconciliations match transactions across sources. Every hop between services goes through a message queue. Figure 1. The platform inside one Kubernetes cluster. The only things that leave are backups, email and image pulls and each goes to a system the bank controls. Five words, one goal These terms get used loosely, so here is what each one meant for us. They overlap and they all serve one goal we wrote at the top of the design: losing any one machine loses no data and stops nothing for more than seconds. Concept The question it answers What it looks like here Reliability Does the system do the right thing, every time? Work is acknowledged only after it is done; locks can't be taken twice; shutdown never drops a file Fault tolerance What happens when a part fails? Replicated database and queues, spread replicas, automatic failover, failures contained to one job High availability How long are users affected? Seconds for a lost server; zero for upgrades and node maintenance Scalability Can it keep up when the work grows? Replica counts follow queue depth; heavy jobs wait for room instead of failing Observability Will someone find out and can they tell why? Alerts by email, searchable logs, dashboards, a daily health report Reliability: no work is lost silently The rule underneath everything else: work moves through the queue and a message leaves the queue only when its work is done. A service that is down or busy leaves messages waiting. Nothing is lost while it recovers. Acknowledge after the work, never before A message broker like RabbitMQ hands a message to one consumer and marks it unacknowledged . It stays in the queue until the consumer says what happened. That gives you three outcomes and each one needs a deliberate answer. Figure 2. Every path out of "unacknowledged" is deliberate. The message disappears only on success; everything else either retries or lands somewhere a person will see it. Here is the pattern in a small consumer that forwards events from a queue to an HTTP endpoint. It acknowledges only after the endpoint answers 2xx and on any failure it puts the message back for another attempt: Python (kombu) def forwarder(endpoint, http_timeout): def on_message(body, message): try: response = requests.post(endpoint, data=to_payload(body), timeout=http_timeout) response.raise_for_status() message.ack() # only now does it leave the queue except Exception: logger.exception("Failed to forward message; requeueing") message.reject(requeue=True) # back to Ready, tried again return on_message Two settings make that safe at the broker. Quorum queues in RabbitMQ drop a message after 20 failed deliveries by default. A consumer that requeues on purpose while its downstream is down (the portal restarting, say) would lose messages after a few minutes of retries, so we lift the limit with a policy and rely on dead-letter queues and alerts for work that truly can't succeed: curl -X PUT "$api/policies/%2F/redelivery" -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -d '{"pattern": ".*", "apply-to": "quorum_queues", "definition": {"delivery-limit": -1}, "priority": 0}' Watch out for the poison message. Unlimited redelivery has a dark side. A message whose processing kills the consumer is redelivered to the next consumer, which dies too. Figure 3. The poison loop we hit on a test server. One large file was redelivered from pod to pod, killing each one at its memory limit. The fix was sizing, not code: the file cleaner's memory limit went from 2 GiB to 4 GiB and a day later the pods still had no restarts. The lessons are general, though: Size memory limits for the largest input, not the average one. An OOM kill is instant: no exception handler runs, nothing is logged by the app and the message goes back to the queue. Alert on OOM kills and on restarts , so a loop shows up in minutes rather than as "the system is slow today". Stream large inputs where you can, so memory stays flat whatever the file size. Consumers that can't stall silently A web service has an obvious health check: send it a request. A queue consumer has nothing to probe and its worst failure leaves the process running. The connection drops, the consume loop blocks forever, the pod shows Running and the queue grows behind it. Figure 4. A heartbeat written only by the loop that does the work turns "running but useless" into a restart. The consumer touches a file at the end of each pass through its loop. Long jobs run on their own threads, so a big file never holds the loop up and the heartbeat really does mean "this process is still taking work": Python LIVENESS_FILE = pathlib.Path("/tmp/heartbeat") while not stopping: try: conn.drain_events(timeout=5) except socket.timeout: pass conn.heartbeat_check() LIVENESS_FILE.touch() # only a working loop gets here Kubernetes checks the file's age. A startup probe gives the process time for its first beat; after that, three stale checks in a row restart it: Kubernetes startupProbe: exec: command: ["sh", "-c", 'f=/tmp/heartbeat; [ -f "$f" ] && [ $(( $(date +%s) - $(stat -c %Y "$f") )) -lt 120 ]'] periodSeconds: 10 failureThreshold: 30 # up to 5 minutes for the first heartbeat livenessProbe: exec: command: ["sh", "-c", 'f=/tmp/heartbeat; [ -f "$f" ] && [ $(( $(date +%s) - $(stat -c %Y "$f") )) -lt 120 ]'] periodSeconds: 30 failureThreshold: 3 Probes can cause outages too. RabbitMQ's usual readiness check, rabbitmq-diagnostics ping , starts a whole separate Erlang runtime to answer. On a busy node that timed out while the broker was healthy, which pulled it out of the Service and refused every client. A plain tcpSocket check is a kernel-level connect with no process to start and it stays reliable under the same load. Locks that can't be taken twice Two reconciliations on the same account at the same time would write conflicting results, so each run locks its accounts first. The obvious way ("check whether a lock exists, then write one") lets two triggers that arrive together both see "unlocked". The lock has to be a single conditional write and it has to record who owns it: SQL (illustrative) -- Take the lock only if nobody holds a live one. Exactly one caller gets a row back. INSERT INTO account_locks (account_id, owner, expires_at) VALUES (:account, :owner, now() + interval '1 hour') ON CONFLICT (account_id) DO UPDATE SET owner = EXCLUDED.owner, expires_at = EXCLUDED.expires_at WHERE account_locks.expires_at Lock several accounts in a fixed order and on a conflict release the ones already taken. Two runs grabbing the same accounts in different orders is the classic deadlock. Every lock-holding workflow releases its locks on failure , on every step. Otherwise a failed run blocks the account until the lock expires. Keep the lock table in the replicated, backed-up database. We moved this state from DynamoDB in the cloud to a Postgres table behind the same interface. Adding a separate store would have meant one more thing to make highly available and back up. Things that must happen once Some work must never run twice at the same moment and Kubernetes happily starts several copies of everything. Database migrations. On a first install, or when scaling up from zero, every portal pod starts together and concurrent migrate runs on an empty database fail on duplicate keys. Each pod's init container takes a Postgres advisory lock first. One pod migrates and the others wait and then find nothing left to do: Python (init container) import django django.setup() from django.core.management import call_command from django.db import connection with connection.cursor() as cursor: # Held by this session until the process exits. cursor.execute("SELECT pg_advisory_lock(hashtext('portal-migrate'))") call_command("migrate", interactive=False) The scheduler. Two copies of a periodic-task scheduler fire every task twice. It runs as one replica with the Recreate strategy, so even an upgrade stops the old pod before starting the new one. Everything else rolls with a surge, so a new pod is ready before an old one goes: # scheduler: never two at once strategy: type: Recreate # portal: never fewer than the desired count during a rollout strategy: type: RollingUpdate rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 } Graceful shutdown: finish the work in hand Pods are stopped all the time: every upgrade, node patch and scale-down. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM , waits for the grace period, then kills the process. A worker that ignores SIGTERM loses whatever it was doing on every deployment. Figure 5. Graceful shutdown has two good endings. Either the work finishes and is acknowledged, or it is left unacknowledged and redone elsewhere. The bad ending, a half-finished file marked as done, can't happen. Python stopping = False def on_sigterm(signum, frame): global stopping stopping = True # finish the current message, then leave signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, on_sigterm) with Connection(broker_url, heartbeat=60) as conn, conn.Consumer(queues, callbacks=[on_message]): while not stopping: try: conn.drain_events(timeout=5) # returns at least every 5s to check the flag except socket.timeout: pass Two details are easy to miss: exec the real process in a shell entrypoint ( exec celery worker ... ). Otherwise SIGTERM goes to the shell, which ignores it and the worker is killed at the end of the grace period with no warning. Know when your framework acknowledges. Celery acknowledges a task when it starts by default, so a task cut off by SIGKILL is gone. acks_late fixes that, but then a task runs again after a crash, which is only safe when every task can run twice. We left it off until every task is idempotent. Component On SIGTERM Grace period File and report workers Stop consuming, finish and acknowledge the job in hand 900s / 1,800s Celery workers Stop taking tasks, finish running ones 900s Ingestion engine A preStop drain: stop picking up runs, wait for its own to finish 1,800s Event forwarder, notifier Finish the current message or email 60s Message broker node Wait until every queue keeps a majority without it (see failover below) Up to the grace period SQL engine worker Finish running query tasks Until its tasks end Fault tolerance Fault tolerance is four techniques working together. Replication keeps the data in more than one place. Redundancy keeps more than one copy of each service running, on different machines. Failover moves the work to a healthy copy when one dies. Graceful degradation keeps the rest working, more slowly if it must, when something can't be replaced. Replication: the database Postgres runs as a three-instance cluster managed by the CloudNativePG operator: one primary and two streaming replicas, each on a different server. Every service connects to one Service name ( postgres-rw ) and the operator always points it at the current primary. We chose it because it uses the Kubernetes API itself to decide which instance is primary. There is no extra consensus store (Patroni-based setups need etcd or similar) and no failover scripts of our own. WAL archiving and point-in-time recovery are built in, it's a CNCF project and it's on OpenShift's OperatorHub, which matters to banks that run OpenShift. Figure 6. Synchronous, quorum-style replication. A commit the application was told about survives the loss of any one server. CloudNativePG Cluster apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1 kind: Cluster metadata: name: postgres spec: instances: 3 primaryUpdateStrategy: unsupervised # roll replicas, then switch over, no human needed smartShutdownTimeout: 15 # default 180s: see below enablePDB: true affinity: enablePodAntiAffinity: true # one instance per server postgresql: synchronous: method: any # synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (...)' number: 1 dataDurability: preferred # degrade to async rather than stop writes preferred rather than required is a graceful-degradation choice. With required , every write stops while no replica is up and a rolling update or a lost server would stop the platform. The window where only one copy exists is short and an alert says when it opens. One default worth changing: smartShutdownTimeout . A stopping primary waits for open connections to close before a replica takes over. Django keeps its database connections open, so the default 180 seconds meant three minutes of errors on every primary restart. Fifteen seconds is plenty. Replication: the message queues RabbitMQ runs as a three-node cluster with quorum queues : each queue is a Raft group copied on all three nodes. A message is confirmed to the publisher once a majority has it, so the queue keeps working and loses no confirmed message, while any two nodes are up. Figure 7. A quorum queue tolerates one lost node out of three. Two lost nodes stop it, by design, rather than risk two diverging copies. rabbitmq.conf # Every node finds the others through the Kubernetes API. cluster_formation.peer_discovery_backend = k8s cluster_formation.k8s.address_type = hostname # Every durable queue a client declares without a type becomes a quorum queue, # so no client code has to change. default_queue_type = quorum # A queue declared while the cluster was still forming gains replicas as nodes join. quorum_queue.continuous_membership_reconciliation.enabled = true quorum_queue.continuous_membership_reconciliation.target_group_size = 3 Setting the default at the broker was the important part. Every service that declares queues kept its code unchanged. Celery was the one exception. Without declaring quorum queues itself, it asks for a global QoS setting that quorum queues reject and it can't consume at all. One setting fixed it: CELERY_QUORUM_QUEUES , read from the environment. Redundancy: copies on different machines Three copies of a service on one server are one failure away from zero. Every workload with more than one replica prefers to spread across servers and has a PodDisruptionBudget , so a node drain (patching, a hardware swap) can't take every copy at once. Figure 8. Spreading puts each copy on a different server. The disruption budget makes a drain wait whenever taking the next pod would leave too few copies. Both come from two small Helm helpers that every Deployment includes: Helm helpers {{- define "chart.spreadReplicas" -}} affinity: podAntiAffinity: preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution: # prefer, so a 1-server install still schedules - weight: 100 podAffinityTerm: topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname labelSelector: matchLabels: app: {{ .app }} {{- end -}} {{- define "chart.pdb" -}} {{- if gt (int .replicas) 1 }} # a PDB over one replica would block drains forever apiVersion: policy/v1 kind: PodDisruptionBudget metadata: name: {{ .app }} spec: maxUnavailable: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: {{ .app }} {{- end }} {{- end -}} Both helpers handle the small case on purpose. Some installs are a single server for user acceptance testing. A hard anti-affinity rule would leave pods Pending there and a disruption budget over one replica would make every drain hang. Failover: when a copy dies The database fails over by itself. When the primary's pod or server is lost, CloudNativePG promotes the most up-to-date replica within seconds and moves postgres-rw to it. Clients see their connections drop and reconnect. With synchronous replication, no committed transaction is lost. The old primary rejoins as a replica when it comes back. The broker needs care at planned shutdowns. Stopping a RabbitMQ node while another is already down would take queues below a majority. So before a node stops, a preStop hook waits until every quorum queue would still have a majority without it, then moves its queue leaders away: StatefulSet container terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 600 lifecycle: preStop: exec: # Wait for quorum without this node, then hand off its leaders. # Gives up before the grace period ends, so a node can still stop # if another one is down for good. command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "rabbitmq-upgrade await_online_quorum_plus_one -t 540; rabbitmq-upgrade drain -t 30 || true"] Stateless workers with long-running state are the hard case. The ingestion engine runs two or more pods, each running reconciliation workflows that hold account locks. If a pod dies mid-run, someone has to notice, mark its runs as failed and free its locks. Nobody else can tell a dead pod from a busy one, so each pod writes a heartbeat row and every pod checks the others': Figure 9. Peer failure detection with heartbeats. Any surviving pod can clean up after a dead one and it frees exactly the locks the dead pod's runs held. The subtle part is not judging others while you're the one in trouble. If the database is down for two minutes, every pod's heartbeat fails and when it returns every heartbeat looks expired. A pod therefore judges others only after its own heartbeats have succeeded for a full timeout period. By then every live pod has written a fresh row too: Python class RunnerHeartbeat: def __init__(self, table, runner_id, clock=time.monotonic): self.table, self.runner_id, self.clock = table, runner_id, clock self.healthy_since = clock() def beat(self): try: self.table.put(runner_id=self.runner_id, expires_at=int(time.time()) + HEARTBEAT_TTL) except Exception: self.healthy_since = self.clock() # our own view is unreliable: start over logger.exception("Runner heartbeat write failed") def may_reap(self): """True once our own heartbeats have succeeded for a full TTL: any live runner has then written a fresh row too.""" return self.clock() - self.healthy_since >= HEARTBEAT_TTL Crash and alert, don't re-run. A dead pod's runs are marked Crashed, not retried automatically. A reconciliation stopped half-way may have written part of its results and running it again isn't known to be safe. Nothing is lost silently: the run shows as Crashed, the account is unlocked and a person is told. Automatic retry is a feature you earn by making the work idempotent. Graceful degradation: fail small, slow down rather than fall over Some failures can't be hidden. The aim then is that they stay small and that overload produces waiting rather than errors. Figure 10. Isolation as graceful degradation. Running each heavy job in its own pod keeps a failure the size of the job. Heavy jobs fail alone. We considered Spark standalone (driver inside the service) and Spark's own Kubernetes mode, whose spark-submit exits 0 even when the job fails. A plain Kubernetes Job already gives a status, a deadline, retries, clean-up and logs. Too much work waits instead of failing. Without a limit, a burst of uploads starts every Spark Job at once. Those the cluster has no room for sit Pending with their deadline running and time out without having run. A queue in front of them (next section) turns a burst into a backlog. Downstream outages become retries. When the portal restarts, the event forwarder's requests fail and the messages are requeued until it's back. Users see their notifications a minute late, not never. Replication degrades to async rather than stopping writes (Figure 6). Telemetry never blocks the app. Services send traces and metrics to a gateway asynchronously. If the gateway or log store is down, the services carry on and the gateway buffers what it can. CPU limits slow a pod down; memory limits kill it. That asymmetry decides how to set each one, as the scalability section explains. High availability: what survives what High availability is the sum of the above, measured from the user's side. We kept one table in the architecture docs that answers "what happens if X fails?" and every design change had to keep it true: If this fails What happens Users notice A database pod or its server A replica is promoted; no committed transaction is lost; services reconnect A few seconds of errors A message broker node Every queue keeps a majority on the other two; no confirmed message is lost Nothing A portal pod or its server The other replicas keep serving; the pod is rescheduled Nothing A workflow pod mid-run Its runs are marked Crashed within 3 minutes, their locks freed, an alert sent That run shows as Crashed A pod being stopped (upgrade, drain) It finishes its current work first Nothing A heavy job Only that job fails, with its error in the run One failed upload The whole cluster Reinstall and restore from off-cluster backups An outage, within the agreed recovery time The object store's disk Not covered by HA yet: restore from the last bucket copy An outage That last row matters. A useful HA table lists what isn't covered, so the bank can accept it in writing or fund the fix. Ours is the object store, which still sits on a single disk. It's on the open-items list the bank signs at go-live. Upgrades are the most common "failure" of all, so they get the same treatment. Setup work runs as ordinary Jobs named after the Helm revision, not as Helm hooks. That way helm upgrade --install --wait --atomic works end to end and a failed upgrade rolls itself back: helm upgrade --install platform . -f values-bank.yaml -n platform --wait --atomic --timeout 20m Scalability on a fixed number of servers In the cloud, scaling means adding machines. A bank's cluster has the servers it has. Autoscaling there doesn't add capacity. It moves the capacity you have to whichever queue is backed up , which pays off when work arrives in bursts, as uploads and exports do. Scale on the work waiting, not on CPU CPU is the wrong signal for a queue consumer. A worker waiting on the database or the object store uses little CPU while messages pile up behind it. Figure 11. Queue depth and CPU for the same worker during an upload burst. Only one of them says "more workers needed". KEDA scales each worker Deployment on its queue length (and for one worker on CPU too, whichever asks for more). It manages the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler itself and it reads queue sizes with a broker user that can see queues but not use them: KEDA ScaledObject apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1 kind: ScaledObject metadata: name: file-cleaner spec: scaleTargetRef: name: file-cleaner minReplicaCount: 3 maxReplicaCount: 8 advanced: restoreToOriginalReplicaCount: true horizontalPodAutoscalerConfig: behavior: scaleDown: { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300 } # 5 quiet minutes before removing pods triggers: - type: rabbitmq metadata: protocol: http host: http://rabbitmq:15672/%2F queueName: file-cleaning mode: QueueLength value: "5" # one pod per 5 messages waiting authenticationRef: { name: keda-rabbitmq-readonly } The workflow engine is different. Its trigger queues empty almost at once into orchestrator runs, so queue length says nothing about its load. It scales on runs waiting or running , through a Postgres role that can do exactly one thing, call a function returning that count: triggers: - type: postgresql metadata: userName: keda # EXECUTE on one function, nothing else dbName: orchestrator query: "SELECT keda_active_flow_runs()" targetQueryValue: "6" # one pod per maxConcurrentRuns One detail for reading the numbers: the autoscaler ignores differences under 10%. With 2 pods of 6 runs each, 13 runs (6.5 per pod) doesn't add a third pod; 14 does. Admission control for heavy jobs Scaling the workflow engine up means more Spark Jobs and those need real CPU and memory. Without a limit, more workflow pods would add load, not capacity. So the Spark Jobs go through a Kueue queue that holds a fixed budget of CPU and memory. A Job is created suspended and starts when the running Jobs leave room for it. Its deadline starts only then, so waiting no longer counts as failing: Kueue ClusterQueue apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta1 kind: ClusterQueue metadata: name: spark spec: queueingStrategy: BestEffortFIFO # in order, but a small job may pass a large one that doesn't fit yet resourceGroups: - coveredResources: ["cpu", "memory"] flavors: - name: spark resources: - name: cpu nominalQuota: "8" # the room kept for Spark beside everything else - name: memory nominalQuota: 24Gi Kueue's admission webhook refuses to create any Job in the namespace while Kueue is down. That covers setup Jobs and backup runs as well as Spark Jobs. A new dependency is also a new failure mode, so Kueue runs two replicas with a disruption budget, only manages namespaces labelled for it and has its own alert after two minutes down. Requests, limits and the throttling trap Every container has CPU and memory requests (what the scheduler reserves) and limits (the ceiling). The two kinds of limit behave very differently: CPU limit Memory limit When exceeded The pod is throttled : it waits for the next 100 ms period The container is killed (OOMKilled) What users see Slowness Restarts, redelivered work (Figure 3) How we set it Enough for the process's real parallelism The largest input plus headroom; alert at 90% The parallelism point caught us. Celery's prefork pool runs four child processes and the workers had a CPU limit of half a core. Four processes shared 500m, so every task ran at an eighth of a core. The Grafana panel "held back by CPU limit" showed it plainly. A 2-core limit matched the pool and the requests stayed small so the scheduler still packs pods tightly. Throttling alerts have their own trap. Throttling is measured as throttled periods ÷ periods . A pod that is idle almost all the time but spikes briefly, a health check that imports a large app, say, can show 60% throttling while using 2% of its limit. Alerting on that ratio alone pages people about pods that are fine. Our alert fires only when the pod is also using a real share of its limit: PromQL (alert rule) ( sum by (namespace, pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{namespace="platform"}[5m])) / sum by (namespace, pod) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{namespace="platform"}[5m])) ) > 0.25 and on (namespace, pod) ( sum by (namespace, pod) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace="platform",container!=""}[5m])) / sum by (namespace, pod) (max by (namespace, pod, container) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{namespace="platform",resource="cpu"})) ) > 0.5 Monitoring and observability without the internet Everything above assumes someone notices when something goes wrong. In a bank there's no internet, often no Slack and the people on call may have no cluster access. Our monitoring had to work entirely inside the cluster and reach people only through the bank's mail relay. Figure 12. Three signals, one place for alerts. Logs are collected from every pod, instrumented or not; traces and metrics pass through one redacting gateway; every alert is evaluated in Prometheus and leaves by email. Collect from everything, redact in one place Logs come from the container log files , not from the apps. The database, the broker and third-party components never send telemetry and they're often the ones that fail. A Vector agent on every node tags each line with its namespace, app, pod and parsed log level. Traces and metrics go through one gateway (the OpenTelemetry Collector). It strips what a bank must not store, such as SQL text, credentials, cookies and URL query strings, once for every service. It also buffers through a log-store restart. Each service is named by its app label everywhere, so its logs, traces, metrics and alerts join on one name. The log store keeps its data in the platform's own object store and Postgres. There's no extra disk to provision or back up. Alerts that mean something Prometheus evaluates the rules and Alertmanager sends email through the bank's relay. A bank's cluster can't reach Slack or PagerDuty, but it always has a mail relay. Each alert links to a runbook: what it means, what's affected, how to check, how to fix, when to escalate. A few of the rules show the thinking. A queue with messages and nobody consuming it. This catches a dead consumer within minutes, whatever the reason: - alert: QueueNoConsumers expr: | max by (namespace, vhost, queue) (rabbitmq_detailed_queue_messages_ready{queue!~".*(retry|dead-letter).*"}) > 0 and on (namespace, vhost, queue) max by (namespace, vhost, queue) (rabbitmq_detailed_queue_consumers) == 0 for: 10m labels: { severity: critical } annotations: summary: "Queue {{ $labels.queue }} has messages but no consumer for 10m" runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example/#queuenoconsumers" A backup that silently stopped. This one alerts on the absence of success, not on a failure. A CronJob that never runs (suspended, a refused admission, a broken schedule) never fails either: - alert: BackupMissing expr: | time() - ( max by (namespace, cronjob) (kube_cronjob_status_last_successful_time{cronjob=~".*-backup-.*"}) or max by (namespace, cronjob) (kube_cronjob_created{cronjob=~".*-backup-.*"}) # a new CronJob counts from its creation ) > 26 * 3600 for: 30m labels: { severity: critical } Duplicates held back. kube-prometheus-stack ships generic rules for the same failures. While our more specific alert fires for an object, the generic one for it is inhibited, so on-call gets one email per problem: inhibit_rules: - source_matchers: [severity="critical"] target_matchers: [severity="warning"] equal: [alertname, namespace] - source_matchers: [alertname="PlatformPodCrashLooping"] target_matchers: [alertname="KubePodCrashLooping"] equal: [namespace, pod, container] Other choices that keep the noise down: Error-line alerts come from a metric, not a log query. Vector counts ERROR lines per app and Prometheus scrapes the count, so log alerts share the routing, grouping and silencing of every other alert. Retry and dead-letter queues are left out of backlog alerts. They hold messages by design. Dead letters get their own alert. A Job alerts only after it has used up its retries. A setup Job that succeeds on its second try stays quiet. Check from the users' side Every pod can be healthy while nobody can log in: a DNS change, a load balancer, an expired certificate. A blackbox exporter fetches the portal, the object store and the other endpoints, both inside the cluster and at their public addresses. It records whether each answered, how fast and when its certificate expires. Vector also turns the portal's access log into request counts and response times, which works behind any ingress controller or OpenShift's router. Mark every change on every chart The first question in an incident is "what changed?". Grafana marks every Helm install, upgrade and rollback and every database failover, on every chart. They come from metrics Prometheus already has (kube-state-metrics exposes the Helm release Secrets and CloudNativePG's exporter exposes the primary), so nothing has to be recorded by hand. A daily report, which is also a dead man's switch Nothing reports to us from a bank on its own. So a CronJob builds a support bundle inside the cluster every morning, with read-only access. That covers pod states, events, recent logs, memory and CPU pressure, queue depths, database activity and Helm values with every credential redacted. It keeps the last 14 bundles in a bucket and emails a short report: each component's state, the problems found and what to do about each. It contains no logs and no data. The report has a second use. When an install's report doesn't arrive by mid-morning, we ask. Its monitoring, its relay or the platform itself may be down and a platform that is down can't send alerts. A signal that must keep arriving is the only way to detect the failure of the alerting path itself. Case study: the disk alert that wasn't about volumes. Volume-filling alerts fired on a single-server install, yet the volumes held little. On k3s, local-path volumes have no quota, so they report the node's whole disk and the disk was 82% full of old container images from months of upgrades. Pruning brought it to 58%. The lasting fix wasn't a cron job, which banks dislike on their servers. It was the kubelet's own image garbage collection, set to start at 75% disk use and stop at 65%. # /etc/rancher/k3s/config.yaml (OpenShift: a KubeletConfig with imageGCHighThresholdPercent) kubelet-arg: - "image-gc-high-threshold=75" - "image-gc-low-threshold=65" High availability is not a backup Replication protects against a machine dying. It does nothing against a bad upgrade, a deleted table or a corrupted volume: those are copied faithfully to every replica within milliseconds. That needs copies stored somewhere else and a restore that is scripted. Figure 13. Replication and backups solve different problems. Point-in-time recovery always builds a new cluster, so the archive it reads from is never overwritten and a recovery that goes wrong can be repeated. Three copies leave the cluster, all to the bank's own S3-compatible storage. That might be a storage appliance or a separate MinIO, ideally in another data centre. It is never the in-cluster object store, which is one of the things being backed up. What How Kept Postgres WAL and base backups CloudNativePG's Barman Cloud plugin: each WAL segment when full or after 5 minutes; a base backup daily 35 days Every database and role A nightly pg_dumpall CronJob: a plain, portable copy for the scripted restore 35 days Every bucket A nightly or hourly rclone copy , which never deletes on the target Never deleted apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: CronJob metadata: name: backup-postgres spec: schedule: "0 1 * * *" concurrencyPolicy: Forbid # a slow night never overlaps the next one jobTemplate: spec: backoffLimit: 2 template: spec: containers: - name: upload command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"] args: - | set -e rclone copy /dump target:$BUCKET/postgres rclone delete --min-age 35d target:$BUCKET/postgres Two stores must agree An Iceberg table has two halves: data files in the object store and a catalog in Postgres that says which files make up each table. Postgres's WAL can be hours newer than the nightly bucket copy. Restored to its latest point, the catalog would point at data files the restored store doesn't have. So the bucket copy writes a LAST_BACKUP marker with its start time to the backup target. Recovery puts Postgres back to that moment, not later. Keeping the marker off-cluster means the consistent point is still known after the whole cluster is gone. For a smaller gap, copy the buckets more often than you dump the database. A restore you haven't run is a hope, not a plan. The restore is a script that scales everything down, refuses to continue while anything else is connected to the database, restores and scales back up. The go-live checklist includes a timed restore drill, so the recovery time the bank signs off on is a measured number. Checklist Every hop between services goes through a durable, replicated queue; messages are acknowledged after the work Memory limits are sized for the largest input and OOM kills and restarts alert Queue consumers have a heartbeat written by the working loop and a liveness probe that checks it Locks are single conditional writes with an owner, released on every failure path Migrations take a lock; the scheduler runs exactly once ( Recreate ) Every process handles SIGTERM : stop taking work, finish, acknowledge, exit; grace periods fit the longest job The database replicates synchronously to at least one replica, on another server Queues are quorum queues; broker nodes wait for quorum before stopping Replicas spread across servers and have disruption budgets, without breaking single-server installs Heavy jobs run in their own pods, admitted when there is room Workers scale on work waiting, not CPU; CPU limits match the process's real parallelism Alerts arrive by a channel the site allows, each with a runbook; duplicates are inhibited Something must keep arriving every day, so a silent install is noticed Backups leave the cluster, the database and object store restore to the same moment and the restore has been timed The "what survives what" table is current, including what isn't covered None of these ideas are new. What changes on a bank's servers is that no provider applies them for you, so each one becomes a line in a chart, a probe or a runbook. Writing them down, with the reason next to each, is what lets the next engineer change one without breaking the others.

title: Build vs Buy in the Agent Era: A Decision Framework for SaaS Teams
summary: Build vs Buy in the Agent Era: A Decision Framework for SaaS Teams Two years ago, "build vs buy" meant choosing between writing your own auth service and paying for Auth0. Today the question is harder. Agent frameworks, orchestration platforms, and model APIs change every few months, and the cost of building an AI agent has dropped while the cost of maintaining one has quietly gone up. If you're a SaaS team asking "should we build or buy our AI agents?" , this article gives you a build vs buy decision framework for AI agents in SaaS you can run in a single meeting. You'll learn: Why the classic build vs buy rules break down for agents Five questions that sort your decision A weighted scoring matrix (with code) to make the decision explicit The hybrid approach most teams end up with Common failure modes on both sides Table of Contents Prerequisites Why classic build vs buy breaks in the agent era Step 1: Split "the agent" into layers Step 2: Ask the five decision questions Step 3: Score it with a weighted matrix Step 4: Estimate the real cost The hybrid pattern most teams land on Failure modes on both sides Conclusion Prerequisites You don't need to be an ML engineer. You do need: A specific agent use case (support triage, onboarding, workflow automation, etc.), not "AI in general" A rough idea of your team's engineering capacity for the next 12 months Basic familiarity with LLM APIs and the idea of tool calling Python 3.9+ if you want to run the scoring script below Why classic build vs buy breaks in the agent era The traditional rule was simple: build what differentiates you, buy what doesn't. It still holds, but agents add three complications. The stack is unstable. Models, protocols, and frameworks are changing faster than most procurement or architecture cycles. A build decision made in Q1 can be obsolete by Q3. Agents are not one component. An "agent" is a model, memory, tools, orchestration, guardrails, evaluation, and observability. You may want to build some of these and buy others. Cost shifts from build to run. Prototyping is cheap. Evaluating, monitoring, securing, and improving agent behavior in production is where the budget goes. Key idea: Don't ask "build or buy the agent ?" Ask "build or buy which layer ?" Step 1: Split "the agent" into layers Before you decide anything, break the agent into layers. Each layer gets its own decision. Layer What it does Typical default Model access LLM APIs, routing, fallbacks Buy Orchestration Multi-step flows, multi-agent coordination Depends Tools & integrations Connectors to your product and third-party APIs Build (for core) / Buy (for commodity) Memory & context Customer data, retrieval, state Build (your data is the moat) Guardrails & policy Permissions, approvals, compliance Build Evaluation & observability Testing, tracing, cost tracking Buy, then customize User-facing channels Chat, messaging, email, voice Buy (usually commodity) This single table removes most of the debate. Most teams discover they want to buy the commodity layers and build the layers that touch their proprietary data and workflows. Step 2: Ask the five decision questions Run each layer through these questions. 1. Is it a differentiator? If customers would choose you because of how this works, lean toward building. If they'd never notice, lean toward buying. 2. Do you own the data and context it needs? Agents are only as good as their context. If the layer depends on deep, proprietary product data, building (or at least controlling) it is safer and often better. 3. How fast is the layer changing? Fast-moving layers, such as model APIs and agent protocols, punish custom builds. If the market is shipping improvements monthly, buying lets you ride that curve instead of chasing it. 4. What is the cost of failure? An agent that drafts a reply is low risk. An agent that issues refunds, edits customer data, or triggers billing is high risk. High-risk actions need tighter control over permissions, audit logs, and approvals, which pushes toward building or deeply configuring. 5. Can you realistically maintain it? Be honest about this one. Building is a commitment to on-call, evals, prompt and model upgrades, and security reviews. If you don't have the headcount for ongoing ownership, a prototype is not a product. Step 3: Score it with a weighted matrix Gut feel is fine for a first pass. A scoring matrix makes the trade-offs visible and gives stakeholders something concrete to argue with. Rate each criterion from 1 (strongly favors buy) to 5 (strongly favors build), then weight it by importance. # build_vs_buy.py from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class Criterion : name : str weight : float # importance, 0-1; weights should sum to 1 score : int # 1 = strongly buy, 5 = strongly build def decide ( criteria : list [ Criterion ]) -> tuple [ float , str ]: total_weight = sum ( c . weight for c in criteria ) assert abs ( total_weight - 1.0 ) 1e-6 , " Weights must sum to 1 " result = sum ( c . weight * c . score for c in criteria ) if result >= 3.7 : verdict = " BUILD " elif result 2.3 : verdict = " BUY " else : verdict = " HYBRID (buy the platform, build the differentiating parts) " return round ( result , 2 ), verdict if __name__ == " __main__ " : # Example: an AI support-triage agent inside a B2B SaaS product criteria = [ Criterion ( " Differentiation " , 0.25 , 4 ), Criterion ( " Proprietary data needed " , 0.20 , 5 ), Criterion ( " Pace of market change " , 0.20 , 2 ), # fast change favors buy Criterion ( " Cost of failure " , 0.15 , 4 ), Criterion ( " Maintenance capacity " , 0.20 , 2 ), # small team favors buy ] score , verdict = decide ( criteria ) print ( f " Score: { score } -> { verdict } " ) Running it prints: Score: 3.4 -> HYBRID (buy the platform, build the differentiating parts) The point isn't the exact number. It's forcing the team to agree on why each score is what it is. Step 4: Estimate the real cost Most build vs buy comparisons fail because they compare the sticker price of a vendor to the prototype cost of a build . Compare total cost of ownership over 12 to 24 months instead. Build TCO ≈ engineering time (initial) + engineering time (ongoing maintenance) + model/inference spend + evaluation & monitoring tooling + security & compliance work + opportunity cost of what the team didn't ship Buy TCO ≈ subscription / usage fees + integration work + customization limits (cost of what you can't do) + switching cost if you leave (lock-in) Two line items are consistently underestimated: Ongoing maintenance on the build side. Agents degrade silently as models, APIs, and user behavior change. Switching cost on the buy side. If your workflows and data live inside a vendor's format, leaving later is expensive. Ask about export options before you sign. The hybrid pattern most teams land on In practice, the answer is rarely pure build or pure buy. A common and durable pattern: Buy model access, channel connectivity, and baseline observability. Build the tool layer that touches your product, your memory/context layer, and your guardrails. Wrap vendors behind a thin internal interface so you can swap them later. # A thin abstraction keeps "buy" decisions reversible from typing import Protocol class AgentRuntime ( Protocol ): def run ( self , task : str , context : dict ) -> dict : ... class VendorRuntime : """ Wraps a third-party agent platform. """ def run ( self , task : str , context : dict ) -> dict : # call vendor SDK here return { " result " : " ... " , " provider " : " vendor " } class InHouseRuntime : """ Your own orchestration, if you decide to build later. """ def run ( self , task : str , context : dict ) -> dict : return { " result " : " ... " , " provider " : " in-house " } def get_runtime ( name : str ) -> AgentRuntime : return { " vendor " : VendorRuntime , " in_house " : InHouseRuntime }[ name ]() Your business logic depends on AgentRuntime , not on any one vendor. That turns a permanent decision into a reversible one, which is the best defense in a fast-moving market. Failure modes on both sides Trust comes from naming what goes wrong, so here it is honestly. When building goes wrong The prototype trap. A demo works in a week, so the team assumes production is a month away. It isn't. No evaluation harness. Without evals, every prompt or model change is a gamble. Reinventing commodity layers. Weeks spent on retries, routing, or channel connectors that vendors already solved. When buying goes wrong Lock-in by convenience. Workflows built in a proprietary visual editor can't be exported. Ceiling hit. The platform handles 80% of the use case, and the last 20% is exactly what your customers care about. Opaque behavior. If you can't inspect traces and decisions, debugging production issues becomes guesswork. Pricing surprises. Usage-based pricing can scale faster than revenue. A quick pre-mortem Before committing, ask the team: "It's 12 months from now and this decision was a mistake. What happened?" Write down the three most likely answers and check whether your plan mitigates them. Conclusion The agent era didn't kill the build vs buy question. It made it more granular. Here are the takeaways: Decide per layer, not per agent. Buy commodity layers, build what touches your data and differentiation. Score the decision. A weighted matrix turns opinions into a discussion you can actually resolve. Compare total cost of ownership, not sticker price against prototype cost. Keep decisions reversible with a thin abstraction between your product and any vendor. Revisit every 6 months. The market moves fast enough that yesterday's "build" can become today's "buy". How is your team approaching this? Did you build, buy, or end up hybrid, and what would you do differently? Share your experience in the comments, especially the failure stories. They're the most useful ones.

title: FlapJax treasury FLAPJAX outflows, 2026-10-28 COT — a chain-only audit
summary: I audited every FLAPJAX transfer out of the FlapJax treasury on 2026-10-28 COT (UTC−5) using nothing but public BNB Smart Chain state. This post is the full working: the day boundary blocks, all 17 transfers, the first BNB funder of every recipient, the operator groups those funders imply, and the transfers I could not explain. Headline numbers Total FLAPJAX sent 2,480,000 Transfers out 17 Distinct recipients 10 Distinct operators (by first BNB funder) 9 Treasury: 0x7c34e9e21ee28a49ff0b84b61774119e6633359f Token: FLAPJAX 0x90c8889f428F9Ebb77BB8f15CAD3a50a9aC680df , 18 decimals 1. The day, in blocks "2026-10-28 COT" is a 24-hour window that does not line up with UTC days, so I did not guess the blocks. I binary-searched block timestamps on a public BSC node until the window was exact. Boundary Block UTC COT (UTC−5) First block of the day 130,221,520 2026-10-28T05:00:00Z 2026-10-28 00:00:00 Last block of the day 130,413,457 2026-10-29T04:59:59Z 2026-10-28 23:59:59 The treasury's last FLAPJAX transfer of the day landed in block 130,409,040 , well inside the window. 2. Every transfer out (17) # Block Time (COT) Tx Recipient FLAPJAX 1 130,289,426 2026-10-28 08:29:31 0xbfc21c77…ef0e7952 0x97cd18b8…2a5a9c 300,000 2 130,289,434 2026-10-28 08:29:35 0x76f4abaa…f9bff77d 0xfb200657…aa24e6 25,000 3 130,289,443 2026-10-28 08:29:39 0xdd2feb71…df9b3da4 0x97cd18b8…2a5a9c 25,000 4 130,289,453 2026-10-28 08:29:43 0x8c630528…d88bb0d9 0xabc2c3da…4ddf62 25,000 5 130,289,462 2026-10-28 08:29:48 0xe468d224…97b2074e 0x3d98800c…bf5f37 25,000 6 130,289,472 2026-10-28 08:29:52 0x7e8f90f4…dc4cad0c 0xdf4ff9d2…db72a5 25,000 7 130,289,480 2026-10-28 08:29:56 0x0c7d758b…9e9b1bb6 0xabc2c3da…4ddf62 300,000 8 130,290,580 2026-10-28 08:38:11 0x825b5c67…df05c8ae 0x97cd18b8…2a5a9c 300,000 9 130,292,025 2026-10-28 08:49:02 0x388a5585…e2763372 0x8c062dc5…53dcdf 10,000 10 130,305,844 2026-10-28 10:32:43 0x69fea445…b021abb5 0xfdf05af8…702ea8 25,000 11 130,305,853 2026-10-28 10:32:47 0x3f4d252e…fd246de5 0xfdf05af8…702ea8 300,000 12 130,305,864 2026-10-28 10:32:52 0x4f591ad8…6cc3f1f9 0xfdf05af8…702ea8 120,000 13 130,329,034 2026-10-28 13:26:40 0x00b7423c…eacd94bd 0xca586965…bda246 150,000 14 130,375,885 2026-10-28 19:18:07 0x41f5bc43…6b283c8e 0xa21fc88b…ad3ee9 250,000 15 130,375,893 2026-10-28 19:18:10 0x36485b49…d88bae37 0xa21fc88b…ad3ee9 50,000 16 130,375,904 2026-10-28 19:18:15 0x9af6e7e8…aff992b0 0xa21fc88b…ad3ee9 250,000 17 130,409,040 2026-10-28 23:26:50 0xcdbada2d…149412a5 0x2ae18c3b…908a02 300,000 Sum of the column: 2,480,000 FLAPJAX . This is the complete set of Transfer events on the token contract with from = treasury inside the block window — read with eth_getLogs , filtered on topic0 = Transfer and topic1 = treasury . Nothing was added or dropped by hand. 3. Recipients and their first BNB funder Recipient Txns FLAPJAX First BNB funder Funding block BNB 0x97cd18b8…2a5a9c 3 625,000 none — never funded — 0 0xa21fc88b…ad3ee9 3 550,000 0xca7ded…094589 128,955,356 0.000164 0xfdf05af8…702ea8 3 445,000 none — never funded — 0 0xabc2c3da…4ddf62 2 325,000 none — never funded — 0 0x2ae18c3b…908a02 1 300,000 none — never funded — 0 0xca586965…bda246 1 150,000 0x7c34e9…33359f 130,097,514 0.000500 0xfb200657…aa24e6 1 25,000 0x7c34e9…33359f 126,835,408 0.000500 0x3d98800c…bf5f37 1 25,000 none — never funded — 0 0xdf4ff9d2…db72a5 1 25,000 none — never funded — 0 0x8c062dc5…53dcdf 1 10,000 0x67f5d4…55dd1f 124,103,796 0.000066 "First BNB funder" is the earliest native BNB transfer into the recipient that exists on chain . I found it by binary-searching the recipient's balance (or nonce) over historical state on an archive node, then reading the transactions of the block where the balance first became non-zero. The funding block is linked above and the funding transaction is in the next section, so every attribution can be re-checked independently. 4. Grouping recipients into operators First BNB funder Recipients Who no BNB funder on chain 6 0x97cd18b8…2a5a9c 0xabc2c3da…4ddf62 0x3d98800c…bf5f37 0xdf4ff9d2…db72a5 0xfdf05af8…702ea8 0x2ae18c3b…908a02 0x7c34e9…33359f (the treasury itself) 2 0xfb200657…aa24e6 0xca586965…bda246 0x67f5d4…55dd1f 1 0x8c062dc5…53dcdf 0xca7ded…094589 1 0xa21fc88b…ad3ee9 The treasury's own first BNB funder is 0x5ba434…9a4268 at block 123,473,817 . No recipient shares that funder, so nothing merges with the treasury through a common upstream wallet. Conclusion: the 10 recipients imply 9 distinct operators — 3 attributable funder groups covering 4 recipients, plus the 6 addresses that no funder evidence can merge. Only one pair collapses: 0xfb200657…aa24e6 and 0xca586965…bda246 were both first funded with BNB by the treasury itself , at blocks 126,835,408 and 130,097,514. Every other recipient stands alone on the evidence available. 5. What I could not explain Six recipients have no first BNB funder, because they have never held any BNB. They are plain externally-owned accounts (empty code), with transaction count 0 and balance 0 at every block I probed, including the present. An account with a zero nonce cannot have spent anything, so a zero balance means nothing was ever sent to it. They received FLAPJAX at an address that has never been able to pay gas. 0x97cd18b8bbb629b17675d868259ea84c0a2a5a9c — 625,000 FLAPJAX in 3 transfer(s) 0xabc2c3daffa4c1963299da225c25f2aa7d4ddf62 — 325,000 FLAPJAX in 2 transfer(s) 0x3d98800c64c345950e1eaaa076d88c12d1bf5f37 — 25,000 FLAPJAX in 1 transfer(s) 0xdf4ff9d2f45f99f11a90b16f277d4b7edddb72a5 — 25,000 FLAPJAX in 1 transfer(s) 0xfdf05af8ddce3621f01713e01721d6e9ad702ea8 — 445,000 FLAPJAX in 3 transfer(s) 0x2ae18c3b2fc18545edd35beeaef97cc2ed908a02 — 300,000 FLAPJAX in 1 transfer(s) No funder evidence links those six to each other or to any other recipient, so I count them as six separate operators — but that is an absence of evidence, not proof of independence. If FlapJax has off-chain records for them, that should override my count. One funder is itself opaque. 0x67f5d43c…55dd1f has nonce 3 and a zero balance today, so its own first funder cannot be recovered by the same balance method. It funded exactly one recipient, so it changes no group count. Recipients were not checked against award history on other platforms (Colony Q78, ugig). Two addresses with different first funders could still be one operator. Nothing on BSC alone settles that, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. 6. How to re-check any row Transfer row : open the tx on BscScan, read the token Transfer log. from is the treasury, to is the recipient, value is the amount in 18-decimal units. Funder row : open the funding block, find the transaction whose to equals the recipient and whose value is non-zero. Its from is the funder, and its value is the BNB shown. Nothing here depends on a private indexer. Balances were read with eth_getBalance / eth_getTransactionCount against historical blocks; transfers with eth_getLogs filtered on topic0 = Transfer and topic1 = the treasury . title: SMBGhost_RCE_PoC

summary: Malicious code on the website of prediction market Polymarket sold some signed-in traders' positions and moved their funds to the hackers on October 29. The code had replaced a page-speed script that the site loaded from an outside company. Polymarket says it is refunding about $2.7 million to 726 affected wallets. Blockchain records show crypto worth about $2.64 million reached the hackers' wallet in under an hour. The replaced script came from DebugBear, whose real user monitoring RUM tool measures how fast web pages load for real visitors. Researchers at Hudson Rock downloaded the malicious file on October 29 from the address Polymarket's site used to load the DebugBear script. They also found a change in Polymarket's site code that removed the DebugBear script. DebugBear's DNS records were compromised through its domain registrar, the company said on X. Its early findings indicate the attack targeted one customer's website. It has seen no sign of a break-in to its own systems, though it is still looking. Researchers at Ohey found a different server answering for DebugBear's web addresses at 18:13 UTC, when the malicious file was still online. Earlier that day, the normal script had been served from Google Cloud Storage. Each DebugBear customer loads its own copy of the script, and the file that was swapped was Polymarket's. title: NetamLoader Malware Targets Government Windows 10 Systems in Asia via .NET Injection
summary: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of what has been described as a "highly sophisticated infection chain" targeting government organizations in Asia. The activity, detailed by Kaspersky this week, targeted a custom Windows 10 build used exclusively by government entities in Asia and involves the deployment of a previously undocumented .NET assembly-loading framework codenamed NetamLoader. The attack has not been attributed to any known threat actor or group. Nor is it clear if the intrusion compromised more than one system and allowed the hackers to steal any sensitive information. The Russian cybersecurity company said the artifact was detected in the first half of 2026, packaged inside a Windows cabinet archive CAB file placed in a directory that stores Windows operating system update packages. It's suspected the operation involved a supply chain attack, in which bad actors compromised a trusted third-party vendor to gain access to downstream users who rely on its services or software. The sample in question features a ".config" file that employs AppDomainManager injection to load arbitrary .NET assemblies. AppDomainManager injection is an adversarial technique used to load arbitrary payloads by hijacking .NET Framework's AppDomainManager mechanism when a .NET application starts. title: reditrap
summary: RediTrap Honeypot RediTrap is a minimal Redis honeypot tailored to spot early attempts to exploit CVE-2025-49844 "RediShell", the critical Remote Code Execution vulnerability described by Wiz Research. The exploit abuses a 13 year old use-after-free bug in the embedded Lua engine: Redis would store the Lua chunk name without first anchoring it on the stack, allowing a garbage collection cycle to reclaim the string while C code still used the pointer. The Redis patch d5728cb fixes the issue by pushing the chunk name onto the Lua stack via setsvalue2s/incrtop before parsing and popping it afterwards, preventing the stale pointer and closing the RCE primitive. Because the published exploit path relies on sending malicious Lua scripts via EVAL, EVALSHA, or SCRIPT LOAD, the honeypot focuses on surfacing those interactions while pretending to be an unpatched Redis node. What it does Listens on the Redis TCP port 6379 by default and speaks a small RESP subset so basic probes succeed PING, INFO, AUTH, etc.. Logs every command to a JSON-lines log file, with extra context for Lua script activity SHA-1 digest, length, token heuristics, preview. Flags script-oriented commands as suspicious and returns safe error replies so untrusted payloads never execute. Mimics older Redis behaviour for example, rejecting HELLO to encourage attackers to continue their workflow. The vulnerable filter runs on restauthenticationerrors, so a forged token authenticates the caller as the first administrator for the entire WordPress REST API, including core routes. That access is then leveraged into full remote code execution. summary: Kali-Linux hacks and setup current release Kali-weekly images: href Download single inode apt install subversion -y svn checkout https://github.com/nu11secur1ty/Kali-Linux/trunk/$inode Introduce: Is Kali Linux Right For You? As the distribution’s developers, you might expect us to recommend that everyone should be using Kali Linux. The fact of the matter is, however, that Kali is a Linux distribution specifically geared towards professional penetration testers and security specialists, and given its unique nature, it is NOT a recommended distribution if you’re unfamiliar with Linux or are looking for a general-purpose Linux desktop distribution for development, web design, gaming, etc. While Kali Linux is architected to be highly customizable, don’t expect to be able to add random unrelated packages and repositories that are “out of band” of the regular Kali software sources and have it Just Work. In particular, there is absolutely no support whatsoever for the apt-add-repository command, LaunchPad, or PPAs. Trying to install Steam on your Kali Linux desktop is an experiment that will not end well. Even getting a package as mainstream as NodeJS onto a Kali Linux installation can take a little extra effort and tinkering. Even for experienced Linux users, Kali can pose some challenges.
